newsitem.title: UK: European buyer rejects costly Algerian condensate.
newsitem.headline: European buyer rejects costly Algerian condensate.

text.p: A major European buyer of Algerian clean condensate has cancelled its contract for October due to high prices, and drastically increased its demand for naphtha as an alternative feedstock, contract holders said on Tuesday.
DOW Europe, with a monthly contract averaging about 200,000-250,000 tonnes of clean condensate from Arzew, has not lifted a single cargo in October.
Negotiations over November prices with state oil company Sonatrach, due to take place in London this week, also risk collapse again, contract holders added.
DOW Europe and Sonatrach officials declined to comment.
Algeria exports around 1.5 million tonnes per month of clean condensate, mostly to the United States and Brazil, but also to European petrochemical and oil companies.
The four European contract holders, DOW, DSM, BP and Elf, together lift around 550,000 tonnes per month.
DOW has replaced its regular condensate imports with naphtha, and traders said this extra demand could continue to be a major bullish influence on naphtha prices for another month.
"That's what everyone wants to know. If DOW takes another 250,000 tonnes of naphtha, it makes a big difference obviously," said a naphtha trader.
Recent high prices for gas oil, which makes up part of the Algerian condensate price formula, is one reason for the collapse of price talks in October, contract holders said.

The formula is made up of 60.45 percent naphtha, 21.5 percent gas oil and 15 percent jet, minus a discount which is negotiated monthly. The formula price usually works out to be cheaper than naphtha, but in October it was more expensive.
"They were not willing to give a rebate to make the price naphtha minus. They came back with a price of naphtha plus. We think that is crazy," said a contract holder.
In October, at least one European customer accepted about $12 per tonne discount to the formula, while others managed to limit their formula to naphtha prices only.
"At least that (naphtha-related) formula is directly affected by the performace of the product and not sucked up by other products," one such contract holder said.
Condensate occurs naturally, like crude oil, but is much lighter. It can be cracked as a petrochemical feedstock, distilled as crude oil, or split to make gas oil and jet fuel.

A trader familiar with Sonatrach negotiations said petrochemical companies would argue that they did not reap the benefit of high gas oil prices from using condensate, while Sonatrach would say they had accepted a gas oil element in the formula until it went against their interests.
One contract holder expected Sonatrach to offer around $12 discount for November, against a European bid at $20 discount. Another held out little hope for the talks:
"I"m sure it will go wrong again in November," he said.
